lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
Date of birth: 3 Mar 1997 | Nationality: Canadian
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Cut the card-dispute form's abandonment rate from 37% to 22% in a four-week A/B test by splitting it into three short steps with saved progress.
- Ran 18 moderated usability sessions a quarter from a recruiting panel of 400 customers, so every major release was tested with real account holders before launch.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Raised the onboarding flow's System Usability Scale score from 68 to 104 across two rounds of moderated testing with 20 customers.
- Validated the redesigned app navigation's findability with an open card sort of 30 customers before it shipped.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Apr 2020 - Feb 2022
- Ran the monthly patient survey and rebuilt its reporting dashboard, cutting the time from survey close to published findings from 3 weeks to 4 days.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Wrote the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Championed an inclusive, human-centered design approach to transit wayfinding that delivered meaningful, user-first outcomes.
- Cut median route-finding time from 90 to 60 seconds, a 50% improvement, by adding audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA)
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interveiws, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: Check that the portfolio link goes directly to relevant UX research work.
items.because: The projects and outcomes on the résumé should be easy to verify there.

items.says: Remove the date of birth and nationality unless an application requires them.
items.because: They generally aren’t needed on a US résumé and can introduce bias.

items.says: If space is tight, remove the education location.
items.because: It is less valuable than the degree and dates.

items.says: Clarify whether 37% and 22% were the A/B test’s control and variant results.
Clarify whether you led the research, the design change, or both.
Replace or qualify “every major release” if the sessions did not cover every one.
“Synthesizing” does not fit the sentence.
The research methods did not directly cut support calls.
items.because: The product or service changes need to be distinguished from your research contribution.

items.says: A System Usability Scale score of 104 cannot be right.
State what the two testing rounds measured if you retain the comparison.
An open card sort does not directly validate findability in the proposed navigation.
items.because: It can inform grouping and labels, but findability requires an appropriate test.

items.says: Clarify how testing informed the shipped design.
Clarify how the post-launch sign-up figures were measured and avoid an unsupported causal “raised.”
items.because: A before-and-after comparison alone may not establish causation.

items.says: Put the strongest, defensible Pinegrove outcomes before activity counts.
items.because: Once corrected, the onboarding and abandonment results are likely more compelling.

items.says: Specify whether automation, a changed reporting process, or both saved time.
Clarify your role in turning interview findings into the two-way text reminder.
items.because: Otherwise the missed-appointment reduction reads as entirely attributable to the interviews.

items.says: Clarify whether the setup-time comparison is for a typical study.
Clarify whether other process changes contributed to the setup-time reduction.
Indicate how and over what period the 30% reduction was measured, if known.
Remove the broad “inclusive, human-centered” claim or support it with a specific action or result.
items.because: It adds little beside the two measurable bullets.

items.says: Going from 90 to 60 seconds is a 33% reduction in time, not 50%.
Give enough testing context to show what was compared.
Going from 65% to 85% is a 20-percentage-point increase, not a 20% relative increase.
Explain the basis for the percentages with 12 participants, if possible.
Clarify whether the two transit results came from the same test.
items.because: Both credit the same features and could appear to be independent validations.

items.says: Clarify the source of the phone-booking figures.
Avoid implying the redesign was the sole cause of the drop in phone bookings unless you can support that.
Be able to explain how each of the six issues was identified and resolved.
Correct the typo “interveiws.”
List A/B testing only if you can discuss your role in designing, analyzing, or interpreting a test.
items.because: Working on a product that ran a test is not enough.
